Mitigation Maintain strict inbound firewall policies (such as Windows Defender Firewall) blocking external traffic on port 7782. This is already the case by default on standard Windows installations. title: Why threat hunting should matter to every board
summary: Monitoring alone cannot detect every threat. Proactive threat hunting can expose gaps in defences and help organisations learn from others facing common threats.
body: Monitoring alone cannot detect every threat. Proactive threat hunting can expose gaps in defences and help organisations learn from others facing common threats.
Boards should have confidence that their organisation can detect and investigate emerging cyber threats, including activity that existing security alerts may miss.

Organisations use a range of cyber security controls. These can include security products, receive threat intelligence and monitor alerts from trusted providers. Many have well-developed processes for responding to known threats. But these measures can’t tell you everything about your ability to detect an attack.
When a new attacker technique is identified, ask: could we detect this technique if it was used against us?
If your organisation can’t answer that question, it may have gaps in its visibility or detection capability.

As attackers use AI to operate at greater speed and scale, identifying and addressing these gaps becomes increasingly important. Organisations need to be able to identify signs of malicious activity early, rather than relying solely on detecting an attack once its effects become apparent.
Threat hunting can help organisations test their ability to detect relevant attacker activity and expose gaps in their defences.

This blog is for boards of organisations that monitor their systems for cyber threats, either themselves or through a third-party provider. It explains why threat hunting matters as threats evolve, and how boards can support their organisation to learn from what it finds and turn those insights into stronger cyber defences.

Security monitoring is fundamental to effective cyber defence. It helps organisations identify potentially malicious activity using established detections and alerts. But not every threat will trigger an existing alert. This is where threat hunting can help.

Threat hunting is the proactive search for signs of cyber threats or intrusion that existing security rules and alerts may have missed. A hunt starts with a question or hypothesis, based on factors such as attacker behaviour or threat intelligence, and uses available security data to look for evidence. Threat hunting complements security monitoring; it doesn’t replace it.

Cyber defenders have traditionally made extensive use of indicators of compromise (IoCs), such as malicious IP addresses, domains, file hashes, or malware signatures. These are useful but they can change quickly.

Attacker behaviours can be more enduring. Security professionals describe these behaviours as tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs). Put simply, TTPs describe how an attacker operates, rather than what specific tools or infrastructure they use.

An IP address may change overnight. A technique for moving through a network may remain relevant for much longer. Focusing on attacker behaviour can therefore provide a more durable basis for detection.
Threat hunting allows defenders to use knowledge of these behaviours to ask whether they can see evidence of them in their own environment.
For more detail on how threat hunting works in practice, including the use of attacker TTPs, read our blog on observability and threat hunting.
You can’t hunt what you can’t see
Threat hunting depends on observability: having a clear and detailed view of what is happening across your organisation’s networks, systems and services.

To investigate whether a particular attacker technique could be present, defenders need the right security data. Systems need to record relevant activity, and defenders need access to that data. Without it, they may be unable to see evidence that a technique has been used.

This means a threat hunt can reveal more than malicious activity. It can also identify gaps in an organisation's visibility and detection capability. For example, a hunt may show that defenders don’t have the data they need to determine whether a particular attacker technique has been used.
For boards, that is valuable information. Even when a hunt finds no evidence of malicious activity, it can reveal where the organisation needs better visibility or stronger detection capabilities.

Those findings should feed back into the organisation’s defences, for example by improving the security data available to defenders, strengthening detections, or addressing other weaknesses identified by the hunt.

Responsibility for cyber defence is often spread across different teams, including security operations, infrastructure, technology, risk and governance functions. Boards need assurance that those teams can turn information about emerging threats into action, and that gaps in visibility or detection are identified, owned and addressed.
Boards don't need to understand the technical details of threat hunting or conduct hunts themselves. They should ask questions that test whether the organisation has an effective capability:
Which attacker techniques are most relevant to our organisation?
Can our defenders detect or investigate those techniques in our environment?
Do our defenders have the security data and visibility they need to investigate them?
When they identify gaps in visibility or detection, who is responsible for addressing them?
How do we know whether those gaps are being addressed and our ability to detect threats is improving?
Are our defenders learning from and collaborating with other organisations facing similar threats?
Boards should look for evidence, rather than relying on reassurance alone. This could include:
examples of relevant attacker techniques the organisation has tested its visibility and detection capability against
what has been done to address them
Over time, boards should be able to see whether those gaps are being closed and the organisation’s ability to detect relevant threats is improving.
Build on the capability you already have
Effective threat hunting doesn’t necessarily require a new threat-hunting team. Organisations may already have people, data and security functions that can provide much of the capability they need.
A useful starting point is to understand what already exists and where the gaps are. For example:
do defenders have the security data they need?
can they use that data to investigate attacker techniques across the organisation's systems?
is there a clear process for acting on gaps that hunts identify?

Organisations should also consider how they use the threat intelligence they receive. Threat intelligence is most valuable when defenders can act on it, for example by turning knowledge of relevant attacker behaviour into questions they can test against their own systems.

Where skills or capability are limited, organisations should consider how existing security providers and trusted practitioner communities can support them, rather than assuming they need to build a new team.
Organisations often face common adversaries, vulnerabilities and technologies. It therefore makes little sense for every organisation to solve every detection problem independently.

Sharing knowledge of attacker behaviour, relevant threat intelligence and approaches to threat hunting can help defenders build a broader picture of common threats, learn from each other and tackle security problems they have in common.
The NCSC encourages organisations to engage with defender communities, where they can exchange insights, discuss emerging threats and learn from real-world incidents.

What one organisation learns from investigating an attacker technique may also help others facing the same threat. Sharing these insights can improve the ability of individual organisations and the wider community to detect and respond to malicious activity.

Organisations can also learn from other defenders through sector-based Information Sharing and Analysis Centres (ISACs) and industry forums. Commercial threat intelligence providers can be another source of information about relevant threats.
Focus on capability, not the solution

For boards, the question is not whether to commission a particular threat-hunting product or create a new team. It is whether the organisation can investigate relevant attacker behaviour, identify gaps in its ability to detect threats, and act on what it learns.
Ask your defenders how they know they could detect the attacker techniques most relevant to your organisation, what gaps they have found, and what they are doing about them.

body: On October 21, 2026, the Node.js project released security updates addressing a critical vulnerability in the Brotli decoder bundled with Node.js, commonly referred to as "Node2Shell" (tracked as CVE-2026-111497). The vulnerability is an out-of-bounds write that could allow a remote attacker to cause memory corruption and potentially execute arbitrary code. This advisory covers the status of impact of various Siemens software products. Siemens has released new versions for the affected products and recommends to update to the latest versions.
The following versions of Siemens Desigo, Gridscale are affected:
Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Critical Manufacturing, Energy, Information Technology
Vendor fix Install the latest .NET security updates via Windows Update.
Vendor fix Install the latest .NET security updates via Windows Update.
Vendor fix Update to V5.4 or later version
Vendor fix Update to V36.8.0 or later version
Siemens ProductCERT reported this vulnerability to CISA.

Operators of critical power systems (e.g. TSOs or DSOs) worldwide are usually required by regulations to build resilience into the power grids by applying multi-level redundant secondary protection schemes. It is therefore recommended that the operators check whether appropriate resilient protection measures are in place. The risk of cyber incidents impacting the grid's reliability can thus be minimized by virtue of the grid design. Siemens strongly recommends applying the provided security updates using the corresponding tooling and documented procedures made available with the product. If supported by the product, an automated means to apply the security updates across multiple product instances may be used. Siemens strongly recommends prior validation of any security update before being applied, and supervision by trained staff of the update process in the target environment. As a general security measure Siemens strongly recommends to protect network access with appropriate mechanisms (e.g. firewalls, segmentation, VPN). It is advised to configure the environment according to our operational guidelines in order to run the devices in a protected IT environment. Recommended security guidelines can be found at: https://www.siemens.com/gridsecurity
For further inquiries on security vulnerabilities in Siemens products and solutions, please contact the Siemens ProductCERT: https://www.siemens.com/cert/advisories
The use of Siemens Security Advisories is subject to the terms and conditions listed on: https://www.siemens.com/productcert/terms-of-use.
CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities.
Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet.
Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks.

When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices.
CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures.

CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies.
CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets.

Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies.
Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents.

title: NCSC scheme will help critical organisations test their cyber defences
summary: New NCSC Cyber Adversary Simulation scheme will help critical organisations strengthen their resilience through rigorous, real-world testing by trusted providers.
body: New NCSC Cyber Adversary Simulation scheme will help critical organisations strengthen their resilience through rigorous, real-world testing by trusted providers.
The NCSC has launched a new Cyber Adversary Simulation (CyAS) scheme.
The scheme is designed to help strengthen national cyber resilience, supporting the UK's most critical organisations, as well as overseeing bodies.

The scheme assures suppliers of cyber adversary simulation services, helping organisations identify trusted providers to test their defences and their ability to prevent, detect and respond to realistic simulated cyber attacks.

Like all NCSC Industry Assurance schemes, CyAS draws on the NCSC’s expertise as the UK’s National Technical Authority for cyber security. Commercial providers are assessed against an NCSC-defined standard, giving organisations confidence that they are buying services that meet recognised requirements.

A key feature of the CyAS methodology is that providers conduct reconnaissance to understand the customer’s technology, exposure and threat landscape. This is then used to develop realistic, customer-specific attack plans. Testers adopt an adversarial mindset and use appropriate tools and techniques to achieve agreed objectives, rather than being driven by commercially procured threat intelligence or constrained by documented tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs).

The scheme complements other NCSC frameworks that support cyber regulation, including the Cyber Assessment Framework (CAF) and the associated Cyber Resilience Audit (CRA) scheme. Together, these frameworks will help organisations - particularly larger organisations, those operating in critical national infrastructure and government - build a clearer picture of their cyber security and resilience.

They also give Cyber Oversight Bodies a trusted way to gather evidence of resilience across the sectors they oversee. This supports consistency, shared learning and a stronger understanding of cyber risk.
Speaking at the launch, the NCSC’s Chief Technology Officer Ollie Whitehouse said:

You cannot improve what you do not know. That is why I am delighted to see the launch of the Cyber Adversary Simulation scheme. By enabling rigorous, realistic end to end assessments by the very best adversary simulation experts, CyAS will help organisations build a clearer picture of how they would stand up to genuine cyber attacks and take action to strengthen their security and resilience.“Ultimately, stronger resilience across the UK helps prepare the country for crisis by protecting the essential services we all rely on every day from the most pressing threats.

Moving beyond traditional pen testing and auditing of controls, the CyAS service enables organisations to practically test their cyber defences, ensuring they are able to protect, detect and respond to cyber attacks.

CyAS has been developed in partnership with Cyber Oversight Bodies, including regulators and Lead Government Departments, to establish a common core standard and a more consistent approach to demonstrating cyber resilience.
The scheme will initially operate as a Minimum Viable Product (MVP), enabling the NCSC to test demand, refine the methodology and build confidence before moving towards a fuller operating model.
You can find a full list of assured service providers on the schemes ‘Find a Provider’ page.

body: CISA has added six new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.
CVE-2026-20320 Cisco BroadWorks Improper Restriction of XML External Entity Reference Vulnerability
CVE-2026-111560 Barracuda Networks Multiple Products OS Command Injection Vulnerability
CVE-2026-111793 Openwave Messaging Limited Webtop Media Transcoder Incorrect Resource Transfer Between Spheres Vulnerability
CVE-2026-116606 Barracuda Networks Email Security Gateway (ESG) Authentication Bypass Using an Alternate Path or Channel Vulnerability
CVE-2026-124194 Microsoft Office Outlook Missing User Interaction for Potentially Unsafe Action Vulnerability
These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

CVE-2026-116779 SignalWire FreeSwitch Code Injection Vulnerability
CVE-2026-123158 OpenBSD OpenSSH Unexpected Status Code or Return Value Vulnerability
CVE-2026-123218 IBM Aspera Faspex Incorrect Authorization Vulnerability
These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

title: Post-Quantum Questions to Ask Your Vendors
summary: CISA, the Australian Signals Directorate’s Australian Cyber Security Centre (ASD’s ACSC) and the National Security Agency (NSA) released joint guidance and an accompanying quick-reference list to help organizations assess vendor readiness…
body: CISA, the Australian Signals Directorate’s Australian Cyber Security Centre (ASD’s ACSC) and the National Security Agency (NSA) released joint guidance and an accompanying quick-reference list to help organizations assess vendor readiness for transitioning to post-quantum cryptography (PQC). As quantum computing advances, widely used public-key cryptography will become vulnerable to compromise from cryptographically relevant quantum computers (CRQCs). To protect their systems and data, organizations must plan for and transition to PQC—which includes algorithms capable of withstanding both classical computing and quantum-enabled threats—before CRQCs become available.

Many organizations rely on third-party vendors for managed services, cloud capabilities, and other cryptography-dependent products and services. Cryptography is also embedded in systems and devices that are difficult to update, tied to long asset lifecycles, and require vendor support or replacement—such as industrial control systems and Internet of Things (IoT) devices. Reliance on vendors means that effective PQC transition depends on vendor readiness, and early, structured engagement with these vendors is critical to planning efforts.

Organizations can use the vendor-neutral questions outlined in this guidance to determine whether a vendor understands quantum-related risks, maintains transparency over its cryptographic implementations, and supports a secure, cost-effective and timely transition to PQC.
Visit CISA’s PQC Initiative page for additional resources.

title: US Government Partners Urge Hardening Industrial Refrigeration and Cold Chain Monitoring Systems
summary: Overview The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), Health and Human Services (HHS), U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), and the Department of Transportation (DoT)—hereafter…
body: The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), Health and Human Services (HHS), U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), and the Department of Transportation (DoT)—hereafter referred to as “the authoring organizations”—are aware of malicious cyber activity targeting industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring systems globally. Organizations in the Healthcare and Public Health, Chemical, Food and Agriculture, and Transportation Systems Sectors widely use these systems, including in refrigerated transport services, for automated and remote monitoring of temperatures, continuous temperature logging, defrost cycle management, and energy optimization.

The authoring organizations urge owners and operators to defend against this activity by using strong authentication, keeping systems updated, identifying any systems that are accessible from the internet, removing unnecessary remote access, and securing any necessary remote access.

The authoring organizations are aware of malicious cyber actors targeting electronic temperature controllers and commercial refrigeration controllers in retail grocery and cold storage facilities. The actors may exploit vulnerabilities or weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers to remotely alter settings and force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles, which can cause widespread inventory loss and equipment hazards.
Specifically, the actors may exploit these flaws through multiple vectors:
Upon successful exploitation of the flaws, the actors could achieve the following effects:
Change of temperature, which could: Affect the service life of the system;
Indirectly harm consumers if products are consumed after unsafe storage.
Loss of visibility into current temperatures (a denial-of-view condition).

The authoring organizations urge owners and operators to immediately take the following actions. These mitigations align with the Cross-Sector Cybersecurity Performance Goals (CPGs), developed by CISA and the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). The CPGs provide a minimum set of practices and protections that CISA and NIST recommend all organizations implement:

Eliminate public internet exposure: Do not expose control system devices and/or systems, particularly controller panels, to the internet [CPG 3.S]. Should remote access be necessary, protect it by using a firewall or edge device and updating it to the latest version to reduce security vulnerabilities. See CISA’s Internet Exposure Reduction Guidance and Defend the Edge: The Critical Importance of Edge Device Security for additional guidance on securing edge devices.
Isolate operational technology (OT) devices: Create a dedicated OT virtual local area network (VLAN) to separate OT devices from business networks [CPG 3.I].

Enforce credential security: Change default passwords [CPG 3.A], strengthen passwords, and implement strong password policies [CPG 3.B]. Further, implement phishing-resistant multifactor authentication wherever feasible [CPG 3.F].

Apply patches: Keep device firmware up to date and establish a structured lifecycle management process to identify, retire, and replace legacy devices that are at end of life (EOL) and no longer supported by the manufacturer [CPG 2.A, 2.B]. See CISA’s BOD 26-04: Implementation Guidance for Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk and BOD 26-02: Mitigating Risk From End-of-Support Edge Devices for additional guidance.
Restrict access: Define and maintain device and IP address allowlisting, limiting access to only those devices and IP addresses authorized to make changes [CPG 3.H].
Have reliable backups: Maintain current backups offsite and offline and test them [CPG 3.O].

Monitor and report: Enable logging [CPG 3.Q] and regularly review logs for unexpected activity. For OT assets where logs are non-standard or not available, collect network traffic and communications between the assets.
Review setpoint ranges: Define and maintain reasonable setpoint limits for devices operating downstream of controllers to stay within safe ranges and establish alerting for deviations.

The authoring organizations strongly urge industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring system owners and operators to secure remote access to their OT systems. To strengthen system security, owners and operators should review the following resources and implement recommended mitigations:

title: Artificial intelligence and cyber intrusion
summary: An NCSC assessment that examines current AI-enabled threat trends and projections of the threat landscape to 2028.
body: An NCSC assessment that examines current AI-enabled threat trends and projections of the threat landscape to 2028.

NCSC Assessment (NCSC-A) is the authoritative voice on the cyber threat to the UK. We combine source information – classified intelligence, industry knowledge, academic material and open source – to provide independent key judgements that inform policy decision making, to improve UK cyber security. We work closely with government, industry and international partners for expert input into our assessments.

NCSC-A is part of the Professional Heads of Intelligence Assessment (PHIA). PHIA leads the development of the profession through analytical tradecraft, professional standards, to build and sustain a cross-government community.
NCSC Assessment uses the PHIA probability yardstick every time we make an assessment, judgement or prediction. The terms used correspond to these likelihood ranges:
This assessment examines current AI-enabled threat trends and projections of the threat landscape to 2028 through three scenarios.

The scenarios are assessed to be plausible possibilities in the medium-term but are not predictions. Instead, they are designed to provide insights into the potential trajectories of AI-driven cyber threats and inform the development of proactive security strategies. Development in AI capability and its application to cyber operations is changing quickly. The prospect for surprise is high.
1 Baseline scenario:Increased global threat from AI-cyber capability
2 Pessimistic scenario:AI-cyber capability proliferation far outstrips the UK’s defensive ability
3 Optimistic scenario:AI-cyber development slows, allowing the UK to develop robust countermeasures

By 2028, it is highly likely that Russia, China and other nation states will routinely use AI-cyber to achieve their geopolitical goals, with the UK facing an increase in scale and speed of sophisticated cyber attacks.

By 2028, it is almost certain that many systems will remain vulnerable to attack from AI-cyber tools which identify and exploit system weaknesses, enabling attackers to display less caution over losing an access, as the cost to replace is minimal.

By 2028, it is likely that attackers will apply AI-cyber capability against known vulnerabilities in critical national infrastructure (CNI) legacy technology, and the new opportunities in the attack surface which the deployment of AI tools within CNI allows.
It is highly likely that between now and 2028, AI-powered malware will have been used in a ransomware attack on UK CNI.
To develop the three scenarios in this paper, we have identified five key drivers likely to influence the AI-cyber threat to the UK in 2028:
The pace of development for AI technologies
Baseline scenario: Increased global threat from AI-cyber capability

In 2028, the AI-cyber threat landscape facing the UK has almost certainly increased. Geopolitical tensions highly likely remain high, and nation states are almost certainly leveraging AI-powered cyber capabilities to project power and achieve strategic objectives.

State-sponsored actors, such as China and Russia, highly likely remain the greatest threat, through their developing AI capabilities. China, despite some quality lag in its chip development, has made significant strides in AI capabilities, with a focus on developing its own indigenous technologies. However, the increasing efficiency of AI models has reduced its dependence on cutting-edge western chip technology.

Meanwhile, it is highly likely that Russian cyber actors have leveraged open-source AI models, adapting and retraining them to suit their intelligence requirement needs, rather than developing in-house capabilities from scratch. This approach has allowed Russia to maintain a significant cyber capability without investing heavily in AI research and development. This has highly likely led to an increase in pre-positioning, espionage and intellectual property theft against UK interests.

The widespread availability of AI-powered cyber tools has almost certainly led to a significant increase in the discovery of zero-day vulnerabilities. Defensive AI-cyber tools have reduced the window of a vulnerability moving from zero-day to an n-day vulnerability, and has made patching a quicker process. However, without correct and widespread configuring of this technology, many systems are still vulnerable to attackers using AI-cyber tools to identify and exploit system weaknesses. Additionally, an organisation’s internal patching and testing processes will need to evolve to meet the pace of accelerating vulnerability discovery. Attackers have subsequently displayed less caution over losing an access to achieve an objective, as the cost to replace is minimal. Cyber capabilities are now used for a broader range of activity due to the lower risk involved, making it easier for adversaries to access information and use it operationally.

In 2028, it is likely that attackers will apply AI-cyber capability against known vulnerabilities in CNI legacy tech and the new opportunities in the attack surface provided by the deployment of AI tools within CNI. The use of AI within CNI has almost certainly presented an increased attack surface for adversaries to exploit. UK CNI has likely seen an increased volume of sophisticated attacks as the result of AI-cyber tools, some combatted by defensive AI tools, but implementation of defensive capabilities in UK CNI lags behind offensive ones.
Pessimistic scenario: AI-cyber capability proliferation far outstrips the UK’s defensive ability

In 2028, the widespread availability of frontier-AI capability to all actors, from state-level threat actors to independent neophyte hackers, has led to a significant increase in the frequency and sophistication of cyber attacks worldwide. The UK faces a significant increase in cyber attacks targeting its CNI, industry, government and civil society.

The proliferation of advanced AI-cyber capability has made it increasingly difficult to attribute attacks to specific threat actors. China, as a leading developer of AI-cyber capability, has likely played a role in disseminating advanced capability to other actors, enabling them to hide their activities within the noise. The use of proxies has become more common, further complicating attribution efforts.

A new threat has emerged in the form of an automated cyber actor, using frontier AI, which is no longer under its operator’s control. It is a realistic possibility that such an entity could self-replicate and conduct cyber attacks at will, with no apparent motivation or restraint. The lack of intentionality of such an actor, and the multiple parties affected by such activity, would likely complicate geopolitical issues. This would also likely make more deniable intentional harm caused by adversaries.

The situation is further complicated by the increased commercial availability of AI tools in the criminal marketplace, including jailbroken models. This has widened the availability of advanced AI-cyber capability beyond sophisticated actors to include inexperienced cyber actors, such as novice or amateur non-professionals, who may not fully understand the risks and consequences of their actions.

In 2028, there is more potential for AI to coordinate cyber compromise impacting the physical world, because of the increased cyber-physical interface with more AI-controlled robots, cloud-controlled CNI and greater integration of cyber into physical (such as biological) labs.

The increased activity from non-state actors and immature threat actors has likely intensified geopolitical tensions, particularly where they are perceived to be emanating from a specific country or region. Espionage activity has also likely increased, with AI-enabled espionage capabilities making it easier for threat actors to remain undetected.

The UK’s use of AI-cyber security tools for defensive purposes has helped to mitigate some of the threats, but it is unclear whether this will be enough to counter the rapidly evolving threat landscape. The situation is likely to be worse than is currently known, with many variables and unknowns still to be discovered.
Optimistic scenario: AI-cyber development slows, allowing the UK to develop robust countermeasures

In 2028, UK CNI has an incredibly robust defence against any, and all, cyber attacks from a range of actors using AI-cyber tools. UK CNI sectors are replacing ageing legacy systems with modern top-of-the-line systems that are less vulnerable to AI-cyber attack. The UK’s cyber defence has also been enabled through widespread workforce education on AI and cyber security.

A series of private and public initiatives have been successful in educating the UK population on AI and cyber security. This has produced a workforce capable of deploying AI securely, and aware of the importance of following standard cyber security measures promptly and consistently. Organisations with well-implemented and strong cyber security measures have demonstrated their ability to deal with AI-empowered threats.

The UK’s proactive approach to AI development and regulation has also paid off. It has given the defender an advantage, allowing the UK to catch up with its cyber literacy. The UK workforce, thoroughly educated in AI and cyber, has been instrumental in deploying AI within organisations effectively and promoting a culture of cyber security awareness.

The UK’s robust regulatory framework has led to the development and release of fewer AI models, with a greater emphasis on responsible AI use. This has resulted in a more transparent AI ecosystem, with a better understanding of the capabilities and risks associated with AI.

It is likely that the AI-cyber threat to the UK in 2028 is significantly mitigated. UK CNI is well protected against cyber attacks from a range of actors, including state-sponsored threats and cyber criminals. Furthermore, existing prepositioning efforts from cyber threat actors have been identified and neutralised. Organisations have well-implemented cyber security measures and have demonstrated their ability to effectively deal with AI-empowered threats.

It is likely that the UK’s robust defence measures and responsible use of AI will minimise the risk of a significant cyber attack, despite China and other nation states’ continued development of AI capabilities. The UK’s proactive approach has encouraged other countries to follow suit, leading to a more stable and secure global AI ecosystem.

Artificial intelligence (AI)Artificial intelligence (AI) refers to computer systems which can perform tasks usually requiring human intelligence. Generative AI (GenAI) is a form of AI which is capable of generating new content, such as text, images or video.
AI-cyberAI-cyber refers to the application of AI developments in cyber intrusion capability.

AI systemAn AI system comprises the host infrastructure, management systems, access control systems and programming interface and can comprise multiple AI designs and models.

AI designAI design refers to the mathematical and algorithmic processes and constraints that are used to convert inputs into outputs. They can vary widely, from narrow linear functions to execute single tasks, through to interconnected functionality that executes complex, decision-orientated tasks. An AI model describes the core AI algorithm.

VulnerabilityA vulnerability is a weakness or flaw in a computer system or process. An attacker may seek to exploit a vulnerability to gain access to a system. The code developed to do this is known as an exploit. A zero-day exploit exploits a vulnerability where there are no security fixes available. A zero-day becomes a ‘known’ or n-day vulnerability once a security fix has been issued by the vendor. Exploitation of known vulnerabilities rely on finding systems that have not been updated.

title: Cyber chief: UK facing AI-powered attacks on critical infrastructure within two years
summary: The NCSC warns that ‘tech on the cheap’ has left UK organisations exposed to AI uncovering and exploiting longstanding cyber security weaknesses and calls for urgent investment in resilience.
body: The NCSC warns that ‘tech on the cheap’ has left UK organisations exposed to AI uncovering and exploiting longstanding cyber security weaknesses and calls for urgent investment in resilience.
AI-powered malware highly likely to be used in ransomware attack on Britain’s critical national infrastructure by 2028, new report warns.
Head of GCHQ’s National Cyber Security Centre to warn, as a society, the era of “tech on the cheap” at expense of security is over.
New State of the Cyber Nation report calls on organisations to make “significant changes” to avert future where AI is used against UK economy and society.

The UK’s critical national infrastructure should be braced for a ransomware attack involving AI-powered malware by 2028, a new report published today [Tuesday 3 November] by the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) – a part of the UK’s signals intelligence agency GCHQ says.

The NCSC's State of the Cyber Nation warns that within the next two years, AI adoption by hostile actors is “highly likely” to increase the scale and efficiency of their operations, including ransomware attacks, social engineering, and vulnerability exploitation.

In a speech to launch the report, the CEO of the NCSC, Dr Richard Horne, is set to say that the AI revolution must force UK organisations to reckon with the current state of their cyber security, as new technologies will expose vulnerabilities, failings and underinvestment at an unprecedented speed and scale in the years ahead. The head of the UK's cyber agency will also set out how artificial intelligence represents the critical opportunity to improve the UK’s collective cyber resilience, but that organisations must take urgent action to address foundational investments and weaknesses or risk adversaries exploiting them instead.

The warning comes as the government is investing in the UK's defence and resilience capabilities, including greater investment in cyber defence, while taking action through the introduction of the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill and the forthcoming National Cyber Action Plan to strengthen the UK's defences, deter hostile state aggression, keep essential services running and keep the British people safe.

Alongside calls for organisations to strengthen their resilience, last week the Chancellor also announced greater investment in capabilities to help the UK harness AI for cyber defence, including £60 million into developing the first phase of a national Cyber Shield, £70 million for a new National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (NERV) Centre to identify vulnerabilities across critical infrastructure and the economy, and a new AI Cyber Security Centre of Excellence, ran by the National Cyber Security Centre, in Manchester to develop world leading AI security expertise within government.

This year’s report suggests that the UK is at a point of “enormous consequence” for cyber security and that organisations across the UK must make use of the tools, standards and frameworks that already exist and are evidenced to protect them from conventional and AI-powered cyber attacks.
The NCSC is imploring organisations across the UK to face what Dr Horne is calling “a moment of choice”. In a speech to launch the report, NCSC CEO is expected to say:

In the coming months, we face a real prospect of an unprecedented rise in the number of cyber incidents. But we must be clear that is not because AI has invented new ways to attack us. But because vulnerabilities that have been tolerated for far too long can now be discovered and exploited at a scale that was once unimaginable.“For decades, we have collectively got away with doing tech on the cheap.“We can be a nation where leaders of all organisations actively choose to invest with urgency... And where all organisations make security and resilience a fundamental requirement, not an afterthought.“The collective result would be a source of enduring national strength for us all.

Dr Horne will urge all organisations across the country to “take the responsibility now to make different choices”, including addressing the failure to adequately invest in their technology; not having technology unnecessarily connected to the internet; and making Cyber Essentials the starting point for cyber security, not the end goal, with organisations building greater resilience according to their size, complexity and risk.

He will say that failing to make these choices will result in leaders “having to look their investors, shareholders, employees, customers, suppliers, in the eye and explain...when food isn’t on shelves, lights aren’t on, businesses have gone under.”

In their tenth year, the National Cyber Security Centre plays a more important role than ever before, defending our security on the cyber frontline.“The NCSC's latest annual report shows cyber threats are growing more sophisticated. We're using the power of AI to help stay ahead of those who seek to do us harm, with a new national Cyber Shield and an AI Cyber Security Centre of Excellence.Security Minister Dan Jarvis
